etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin līberātus, past participle of līberō (“to set free, deliver”), from līber (“free”); see liberal.

definitions.definition: To release from slavery: to manumit.
To release from servitude or unjust rule.
To release from restraint or inhibition.

quote.citation: 1991 May 12, “Kidnapped!”, in Jeeves and Wooster, Series 2, Episode 5:
quote.text: Jeeves: Foreign travel often liberates emotions best kept in check, sir. The air of North America is notoriously stimulating in this regard, as witness the regrettable behavior of its inhabitants in 1776.B. Wooster: Hm? What happened in 1776, Jeeves?Jeeves: I prefer not to dwell on it, if it's convenient to you, sir.

definitions.definition: (chemistry) To release from chemical bonds or solutions.
(transitive) To set free, to make or allow to be free, particularly
(transitive, military, euphemistic) To acquire from an enemy during wartime, used especially of cities, regions, and other population centers.
(transitive, euphemistic) To acquire from another by theft or force: to steal, to rob.

quote.citation: 1969, United States. Congress. Senate. Committee on Government Operations. Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Riots, Civil and Criminal Disorders, page 3796:
quote.text: I had proven myself, when I was required to liberate (steal) dynamite, steal cars for robberies, and to perform disciplinary action against party members.

quote.citation: 1986, Jack Hemingway, Misadventures of a Fly Fisherman: My Life with and Without Papa, page 158:
quote.text: For expedience, he intended to use his talents to liberate a few choice bottles from the wine cellars without going through the difficulty of a formal requisition.
He was trying to liberate some funds for the revolution from a liquor store, and he got caught. It was his first time out, and he got flat-ass caught.
